traces.answer: There is no point doing anything less than perfect when you hire your VP of Sales. It's just too important. So if they don't hit the plan their first month, fire them. If they aren't recruiting strong folks under them by Month 2, fire them. If they can't close every big deal themselves -- even when they lose -- by Month 2, fire them. And importantly, criticize them mercilessly until then for failing. Because most won't deliver, period. They'll blame others. Blame marketing for lack of leads. Blame product for being feature poor. Blame anyone else except for themselves for not hitting the plan. But what you really need to do is help them succeed. Help them get there. This is also why I've never made this mistake myself hiring sales leaders. We all make mistakes. The key isn't making fewer mistakes (you're going to). It's knowing how to learn faster from those mis-hires. And learning what to look for after each one. You have to know what worked before, and what didn't. At least, for the next iteration. More here:

Does Jason Lemkin say a great VP of Sales should immediately bring in more sales executives, or that criticizing a VP of Sales who cannot do better is counterproductive?

It’s complicated, and most things in SaaS recruiting really are.

The best VPs of Sales I’ve worked with were all different:

Some hired their entire team themselves by osmosis.  And quickly

Others needed some help here, especially if they’d never been founders before. Some needed a few extra hands to get going. Others didn’t need anyone until later.

Some could hack it for months, even years, without much help

Other good ones couldn’t get anything going without a strong hand up

And … there are plenty of mediocre VPs of Sales that hire tons of folks (often with a lot of help

The mediocre ones do almost nothing except complain, criticize others for not doing well enough
[...]

They're afraid if they bring in someone smarter, better, more experienced, something else, that that'll threaten their job.
A mediocre VP of Sales focuses primarily on process
[...]
They take a lot of time talking about how things should happen, talking about goals, making sure every single goal gets met by every individual. It's very important to set clear goals, but they spend way too much time focused on process. Instead of going out there and helping your team close those big deals, instead of jumping into the tough deals yourself and figuring out why they lost, instead of hiring some of those amazing people ahead of you.
